approved: Customs Tariff Amendment (Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus Implementation) Bill 2018
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change customs duties to put a trade deal with Pacific island nations into effect.
Goods from those countries would enter Australia duty-free, except for alcohol, tobacco and fuel, which would get special rates.
The government expects the deal to cost it almost nothing in lost revenue over the five years to 2020–21.
Sets a zero customs duty rate for most goods from Pacific island nations once the agreement starts.
Adds a new schedule to the Customs Tariff Act with excise-equivalent rates for alcohol, tobacco and fuel.
Updates some existing concessional items in the tariff to keep duty rates consistent with the trade deal.
Importers of goods from Pacific island nations that are party to the agreement.

The Customs Tariff Amendment (Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus Implementation) Bill 2018 was moved for a second reading, amending the Customs Tariff Act 1995 to provide duty-free access for eligible goods from PACER Plus parties, with excise-equivalent duties maintained for consistency with domestic goods. The bill complements the Customs Amendment (PACER Plus Implementation) Bill 2018 and follows the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties' recommendation for binding treaty action.

Labor supported the Customs Amendment bills to implement the PACER Plus free trade agreement with 14 Pacific Island nations, providing preferential duty rates on imports and committing Australia to $23 million in aid for Pacific countries. The speaker criticised the Turnbull government for refusing to commission independent economic modelling on trade agreements, despite recommendations from the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties and industry groups.

The speech supported the PACER Plus implementation bills but argued the agreement primarily benefits Australia through tariff reductions, eliminating tariffs on 91.5 per cent of export lines from Australia and New Zealand and 88.5 per cent of Australian exports, while noting the labour mobility arrangement is the key interest for Pacific island nations.

The speaker argued that the PACER Plus trade bills represent a small but significant step in regional development, stressing that the agreement is not about expanding Australian markets but about providing development assistance and tariff reductions for Pacific island nations. They noted the exclusion of Papua New Guinea and Fiji, called for greater Australian leadership in the Pacific, and emphasised that opening the Australian economy and labour market, including through the Seasonal Worker Program, is the most impactful way to drive development in the region.

The speaker supported the bills implementing PACER Plus, which will cut tariffs on 88.5% of Australian exports to signatory Pacific nations (excluding New Zealand) and remove tariffs on imports from them, with $23 million in assistance. He criticised the government for cutting $11 billion from the aid budget and for refusing to require independent economic analysis of trade agreements, which Labor would mandate if elected.

The minister argued that the Coalition government has refocused foreign aid towards the Pacific and blamed the Labor Party for Australia's half-trillion-dollar debt and the reduction in the aid budget, accusing Labor of hypocrisy for complaining without committing funds. He announced that the PACER Plus agreement, signed by 11 Pacific Islands Forum members, will create closer economic integration and development in the region, and urged Australia to ratify early.
